newsitem.title: USA: Stocks jump as Wall Street toasts Fed no rate hike decision.
newsitem.headline: Stocks jump as Wall Street toasts Fed no rate hike decision.

text.p: Stocks ended sharply higher on Tuesday, as the Federal Reserve's decision to keep interest rates unchanged added more spark to the market's fiery recovery from last Friday's plunge.
The Dow Jones industrial average was up 114.74 points, or 1.47 percent, at 7,918.10 after storming 109 points higher on Monday on the back of Friday's 247-point loss.
The Nasdaq composite index jumped 31.19 points, or nearly 2 percent, at 1,600.71 on the strength of technology stocks.
In the broader market, advancing issues swamped declines 2,026 to 804 on heavy volume of 545 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Wall Street cheered the Fed's non-action, which was seen as a vote of confidence that the economy can continue to grow at a comfortable speed without reigniting inflation.
The Fed left key interest rates unchanged amid clear signs that the economy is growing at a moderate pace with low inflation.

"The Fed did nothing today, and my guess is that they're not going to do anything probably through the end of the year," said Lawrence Chimerine, managing director at the Economic Strategy Institute, a Washington-based think tank.

The central bank last tightened policy on March 25, when it raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points, a move that sparked a sell-off of nearly 10 percent in the blue-chip Dow index. The Fed has since held the line on interest rates.
"We were able to bounce back with the Fed's non-action, the UPS settlement and there was a lot of money flowing into technology stocks," said one trader.
In the bond market, the Treasury's 30-year bond rose 4/32, trimming its yield to 6.51 percent from Monday's close of 6.52 percent. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

The stock surge masked some stormy volatility. The Dow had earlier scored gains of more than 100 points but whipsawed lower in the minutes following the Fed's announcement, losing 75 points, before heading sharply higher again.
Technology stocks sizzled as as money managers, looking for more growth and cheaper valuations, rotated money out of blue-chip stocks and into that sector, analysts said.
"Most of the blue chips have had such strong advances, how much further can they go? The play is to look for growth," said Kenneth Ducey, director of trading at BT Brokerage.

Technology stocks were also helped by news that Bay Networks Inc. expects its quarterly revenues to beat analysts' expectations. Bay Networks rose 3-1/4 to 37-1/8 and was the NYSE's most heavily traded issue.
Elsewhere in the high-tech sectors, Microsoft Corp. rose 4-15/16 to 138-13/16 and International Business Machines Corp. was up 3-15/16 at 107-15/16.
Gillette Co., which tumbled Friday and Monday after it guided analysts estimates down, recouped lost ground as Merrill Lynch raised its rating on the stock. It closed up 2-3/4 to 85-3/4.
Other consumer products companies also snapped back, with Procter & Gamble Co. adding 3-3/4 to 138-3/4 and Avon Products Inc. rising 2-1/4 to 67-3/16.

Some stocks were buoyed by the settlement of the bitter 15-day strike at United Parcel Service. Gateway 2000 Inc., which ships its computers to customers via UPS, rose 2-15/16 to 40-3/8. Retail catalog companies rose, with Lands' End Inc., up 5/8 to 28-1/16 and J.C. Penney up 1-1/8 to 61.

Strong second-quarter earnings from some retailers also boosted that sector. Tiffany & Co. Inc. jumped 2-1/4 to 43 after its earnings beat Wall Street estimates. Home Depot Inc. rose 1-7/16 to 49-7/16 after posting earnings that slightly beat estimates.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 13.52 points to 926.01. The American Stock Exchange index rose 6.63 to 641.22.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 5.99 to 479.54. The average share was up 55 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 8,826.764 up 118.188 or 1.36 percent.
